ures `pqr` (a doubled triangle);
- **hat** (one of each): `p*q`.

Greedy loop (OG:461-573): while features remain — if mirrors and cones both exist, pop a cone and cut a `slice` to the boundary, producing hat `[[slice_n],[cone]]` and pushing `slice_n` onto the kaleido list (OG:482-489); if >3 cones and no mirrors, pop two cones into pillow `[cone1, cone2, tube_n]`, pushing `tube_n` back (OG:490-504); exactly 3 cones → final pillow (OG:505-531); >3 corner features → sheet `[kal0, kal1, slice_n]` (OG:533-546); exactly 3 → final sheet (OG:547-570). Special cases: bare-`mirror` kaleido with exactly two cones → two hats sharing one slice (OG:463-476); one kaleido + one cone → single hat (OG:477-481). Real features (`conePt`/`corner`) are always swapped to the front of each atom's list — `unfoldAtom` "assume[s] we've gotten our features in order of real first, then imaginary" (OG:652). New cuts are unshifted to the **other** end of the list so "new slices are sliced last; this ensures a tree-like structure in the cutting" (OG:448-449).

Examples **[verified by execution]**: `2223` → single pillow `[[],[conePt 2, conePt 3, conePair 1]]`; `34x` → pillow `[[],[conePt 4, conePt 3, cap 1]]`; `3456` → two pillows `[[],[6,5,tube1]]`, `[[],[4,3,tube1]]`; `*34x` → hat `[[slice1],[cap1]]` + sheet `[[corner4, corner3, slice1],[]]`; `4*3` → one hat `[[corner3],[conePt4]]`; `*237` → one sheet.

### 3c. `unfoldAtom` (OG:648-1133) — atoms to Poincaré-disk polygons
Twelve cases (3 sheet + real-corner counts, 4 pillow, 4 hat; OG:652). Thurston's imaginary-angle device: a real feature contributes an actual polygon vertex with angle `p.re = PI/order` (sheets) or `2π/order` (pillows/hats); an **imaginary** feature (`p.im = getLength(feature)`) truncates the vertex into a geodesic edge of hyperbolic length `p.im`, perpendicular to its neighbors. `edgeLength` (OG:588-619) is the generalized hyperbolic law of cosines:

```js
ll = (cp * cq + cr) / (sp * sq);          // cp = cos(p.re) or cosh(p.im), sp = sin/sinh
if ((p.re==0 && q.re==0) || (p.im==0 && q.im==0)) return acosh(ll); else return asinh(ll);
```

The polygon is then walked out with turtle geometry: `poincarePt(d)` = point at hyperbolic distance d on the real axis (`tanh(d/2)`, CA:237-239) and `poincareTurtleMove(last, current, angle, distance)` (CA:459-467) which rotates about the current vertex and translates a hyperbolic distance. E.g. the all-real sheet `*pqr` is the classical mirror triangle with edges `[["mirror",0],["mirror",0],["mirror",0]]` (OG:676-689). Pillows are unfolded as doubled triangles cut open by 3 fresh `cuttingEdge` pairs (OG:807-821 etc. — note the internal half-lengths `cosh(r.im/2)` at OG:829-834 versus the full-length turtle move `r.im` at OG:849: the FD edge for the feature always has full slider length). Hats halve the feature length for the trig, then double it back for the walk (`getLength(b,group)/2` at OG:1027, `q.im*2` at OG:1040). Return shape: `[vertices, edges]`, with the note OG:655-659 that the structure "is kind of dumb and probably could be improved". Some pillow `cuttingEdge` keys get 2 extra points appended — a "wall" perpendicular at a vertex, needed so "the correct generator will be chosen in inversive.frag" when a tube meets the cutting edge (OG:767-772, OG:861-872).

### 3d. `assembleFundamentalDomain` (OG:1195-1382) — regluing
All atoms are unfolded (OG:1208-1210); the first becomes `workingFD` (recentered, OG:1213-1215); its `tube`/`slice` edges seed `openAttachments` (OG:1229-1232, "attachments will always be 'tube' or 'slice'"). Loop (OG:1234-1368): pop an attachment; cyclically rotate `workingFD` until that edge is in front (OG:1240-1244); linearly search the remaining atoms for the matching edge, rotating each candidate (OG:1249-1269); then

```js
if (Array.isArray(nextAtom[1][0]) && nextAtom[1][0][0]=="tube") {
    shift = getTwist(nextAtom[1][0], group)          // OG:1292-1294
}
var mob = poincareMobiusEdgeToEdge(
    [nextAtom[0][0], nextAtom[0][1]], [workingFD[0][0], workingFD[0][1]], shift)   // OG:1295-1296
```

`poincareMobiusEdgeToEdge` (CA:472-491) conjugates both edges to the real axis and inserts `transX = makeMobius([[1,0],[tanh(shift/2),0],true])` (CA:482) — i.e. the atom is slid a hyperbolic distance `shift` **along the shared cut geodesic** before being welded on. For a **tube** the two flanking edge-pairs become colinear merged edges (walls preserved, OG:1301-1334); for a **slice** both copies of the cut edge are simply deleted (`slice(2)` concatenation, OG:1335-1343). Both record an `internalFDedges` entry so the seams can be drawn. The domain is recentered (Euclidean centroid → origin) twice per gluing for numerical stability (OG:1136-1141, 1351-1365), and finally nudged off-center by `poincareMobiusTranslateToO(new complexN(-.001,-.002))` — "and then another nudge" (OG:1369-1374) — general position, complementing the ±.0005 randomization of default lengths ("to put the group into general position by default", WPG:52-53). Returns `[workingFD, internalFDedges, conepts]` where `conepts` is declared but never assigned (OG:1378-1381; WPG:305 "assembledFD[2] will be a list of cone points TO DO").

**[Verified by execution]** e.g. `3456` assembles to a 10-gon whose boundary is 5 matched `cuttingEdge` pairs (the tube seam fully absorbed); `*34x` to a hexagon `[cuttingEdge1, cap1, cuttingEdge1, mirrorRedundant, mirror, mirror]`; `4*3` to the quadrilateral `[mirror, cuttingEdge1, cuttingEdge1, mirrorRedundant]`.

### 3e. `produceGenerators` (OG:1387-1493) — the group
"each edge bounding a presumed-convex fundamental domain gets a single list of circles through which to invert, a single generator" (OG:1394-1396). Output is `sPlanes`: one list of 1–3 inversion circles per edge (compose via `poincareMobiusFromSPlanesList`, CA:831-837, to get the Möbius map). Cases as tabulated in §2; the pairing search for handle/cuttingEdge/band is a brute scan for the other edge with an equal `[key,n]` (OG:1426-1430). `WallPaperGroup_General.updateTheGroupGeometry` then builds `FD = { s: bounds, t: transforms, i: interiors }` (WPG:364-368) where each bound is the `sPlaneThrough` arc of the edge (plus wall sPlanes, WPG:326-336); per the comment WPG:370-376, "FD.s is u_domainData and FD.t is u_groupTransformsData" for the fragment shader.

---

## 4. `countParameters` (OG:266-277) — dimension of the deformation space

Exact code (OG:270-274):

```js
var numParameters = -6 + 6 * hashedOrbifold.handlesN + 3 * hashedOrbifold.crosscapsN
                  + 2 * hashedOrbifold.conepoints.length
                  + 3 * hashedOrbifold.kaleidoscopes.length;
hashedOrbifold.kaleidoscopes.forEach(function(kal) {
    numParameters = numParameters + kal.length
})
```

i.e. **dim = −6 + 6·(#handles) + 3·(#crosscaps) + 2·(#cone points) + 3·(#kaleidoscopes) + (total #corner points)** — the Teichmüller-space dimension of the hyperbolic orbifold. Note the comment OG:267-268: this is "stashed in theGroup.parN but is not really used, except in messages in the gui" — the actual sliders are generated from `parCounts` (WPG:263-284), not from this number. In every case I executed the two agree: `2223` → 2 (conePair_1_l/t), `34x` → 1 (cap_1_l), `*34x` → 2 (cap_1_l, slice_1_l), `3456` → 2 (tube_1_l/t), `22222` → 4 (conePair_{1,2}_l/t), `4*3` and `*237` → 0 (rigid). **[verified by execution]**

---

## 5. How the length/twist values enter the geometry

**GUI plumbing.** Sliders are named `key_i_l` and `key_i_t` (WPG:268, 280), created for `i = 1..parCounts[key]` over `lengthKeys`/`twistKeys` (WPG:263-284). Ranges (WPG:26-29): `LENGTHMINVALUE = .3`, `LENGTHMAXVALUE = 4`, `TWISTMINVALUE = -.5`, `TWISTMAXVALUE = .5`. Defaults: length `2 + .001*(random()-.5)` ≈ 2.0 (WPG:266), twist `0` (WPG:278). `getLength`/`getTwist` (OG:624-637) read `group.guiParams[key[0]+"_"+abs(key[1])+"_l"/"_t"]`, with fallbacks 1.1 and 0 if no such parameter exists.

**Lengths — hyperbolic edge lengths of the FD polygon.** In `unfoldAtom`, every imaginary feature's "angle" is set to its slider value: `r.im = getLength(c, group)` (sheets OG:696, 714-715, 734-736; pillows OG:828, 878-879, 933-935; hats halved then doubled, OG:1027/1040, 1062, 1093-1094). That number is used (a) inside `edgeLength`'s law-of-cosines to size the rest of the polygon, and (b) **directly as the turtle-move distance** for the feature's own edge (e.g. `poincareTurtleMove(y, z, -HPI, r.im)`, OG:705, 728, 849, 905). So `tube_1_l = 2.0` literally means: the geodesic segment of the FD boundary (or interior seam) realizing that feature has hyperbolic length 2.0, meeting its neighbors at right angles (the `-HPI` turns). This is Thurston's imaginary-angle triangle: the vertex is replaced by the common-perpendicular geodesic.

**Twists — offsets along the gluing geodesic.** Three distinct uses:

1. **tube** — `assembleFundamentalDomain` OG:1292-1296: `shift = getTwist(...)` is passed to `poincareMobiusEdgeToEdge`, which inserts a hyperbolic translation `tanh(shift/2)` along the aligned cut geodesic (CA:482) before welding the atom on. So a tube twist is an **absolute hyperbolic translation distance** (in [−0.5, 0.5]) by which one side of the tube seam is slid against the other — a Fenchel–Nielsen twist along the cut.
2. **handle** — `produceGenerators` OG:1438-1444:
   ```js
   if(key=="handle"){shift = getTwist(edge,group)}
   if(shift!=0){
     p1 = v1.applyMobius(poincareMobiusTranslateFromToByD(v1,v2,shift*getLength(edge,group)));
     p2 = v2.applyMobius(poincareMobiusTranslateFromToByD(v1,v2,shift*getLength(edge,group)));
   }
   var centers = sPlanesMovingEdge1ToEdge2([p1,p2],[q2,q1])
   ```
   The source edge is slid along its own geodesic by `shift * length` — a **fractional** twist (fraction of the handle length, so −½…½ spans a half period each way) — before the identification with the reversed partner edge is built. For the structure, I'm planning a hero section with the title "Two Dollars of Symmetry" — a reference to the Magic Theorem's elegant result that every wallpaper group has exactly two orbifold singularities. The narrative arc moves from the interactive experience of dragging in SymmHub (exploring Teichmüller space) through the historical development from Macbeath through Conway's 1992 notation, explaining how the orbifold notation encodes symmetry information.

I'm building out the core sections: a symbol dictionary with mini SVG illustrations showing what each notation element means, then an interactive cost calculator where users input an orbifold symbol and get back an itemized "receipt" showing the χ value and classification (spherical, Euclidean, or hyperbolic). I need to be careful with quotes — keeping any attributed quotes under 15 words and sparse throughout. Conway's thesis references Thurston's work on the dimension formula and Teichmüller space; the key insight is mapping the drag parameters to concrete geometric quantities like cone-pair lengths and twists, tube seams, and cap slices—each corresponding to specific degrees of freedom in the orbifold structure. Adding interactive demos and documentation...

I'm also working through the spherical and polyhedral orbifold cases, establishing validation rules so the calculator can flag invalid symbols like teardrops and catch cases where single digits or unequal digit pairs appear without proper notation markers.

Now I need to implement the parser itself—iterating through characters, handling multi-digit numbers with parentheses, and tracking the kaleidoscope state where a digit following an asterisk represents a corner angle. I'll mirror CGS's parser logic and compute the Euler characteristic using cost formulas: cone angles cost (n-1)/n, corner angles cost (n-1)/2n, and both asterisks and crosses add 1, while circles add 2. class=\"hero prose\" style=\"max-width:880px\">\n  <div class=\"eyebrow ink\" style=\"margin-top:0\">SymmHub &nbsp;·&nbsp; hyperbolic symmetry lab &nbsp;·&nbsp; Bulatov · Goodman-Strauss · Vorthmann</div>\n  <h1>Two Dollars of Symmetry</h1>\n  <p class=\"sub\">In SymmHub you can type <span class=\"sym\">3456</span> into a box, get a hyperbolic wallpaper,\n  and then <em>grab an edge of its fundamental domain and drag it</em>. This page explains what that drag\n  actually is: Conway's orbifold notation, the Magic Theorem that prices every symmetry at exactly two\n  dollars, a lost 1994 Princeton thesis, and the Teichm&uuml;ller coordinates hiding behind a yellow highlight.</p>\n</div>\n\n<div class=\"prose\">\n\n<div class=\"eyebrow phy\">Part I &nbsp;·&nbsp; The idea</div>\n<h2>A symmetry is a way of folding the plane</h2>\n\n<p>Take an infinitely repeating pattern — bathroom tiles, an Escher print, a hyperbolic\ntiling in the Poincar&eacute; disk. Its symmetry group is the set of motions that leave it looking\nuntouched. The classical way to study the group is to list generators and relations. The\n<em>orbifold</em> way, due to William Thurston, is to do something more physical: fold the\npattern up along all of its symmetries, until no two equivalent points remain. What is left\nis a small, curved scrap of surface — the <b>orbifold</b> (from <i>orbit&nbsp;+ manifold</i>,\na name chosen by a vote in Thurston's Princeton class). Everything about the group is written\non that scrap:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>a point where the pattern spins $n$ times becomes a <b>cone point</b> of order $n$ — the paper is rolled into a cone;</li>\n<li>a mirror line becomes a <b>boundary</b> of the scrap; corners where mirrors cross become <b>corner points</b>;</li>\n<li>a glide reflection — symmetry with no mirror and no rotation, Conway called it a <b>miracle</b> — sews a cross-cap into the scrap;</li>\n<li>plain translations with nothing else to show for themselves roll the scrap into a <b>handle</b> — Conway's <b>wonder</b>.</li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>John Conway's notation, introduced around 1990 and refined with Daniel Huson (2002) and in\n<i>The Symmetries of Things</i> (2008, with Heidi Burgiel and Chaim Goodman-Strauss), simply\nspells the scrap: one character per feature. Conway was careful about the pedigree — he described\nhis symbol as an elegant repackaging of A.&nbsp;M. Macbeath's 1967 &ldquo;signature&rdquo; for\nnon-Euclidean crystallographic groups, expressed in Thurston's orbifold language.</p>\n\n</div>\n\n<div class=\"glyphrow\">\n  <div class=\"glyph\"><div class=\"g\" style=\"color:#1F4E79\">o</div><div class=\"nm\">wonder · handle</div>\n    <p>pure translations; rolls the orbifold into a torus handle</p><div class=\"price\">costs <b>$2</b></div></div>\n  <div class=\"glyph\"><div class=\"g\" style=\"color:#AA00E1\">n</div><div class=\"nm\">gyration · cone point</div>\n    <p>an $n$-fold rotation center not on a mirror</p><div class=\"price\">costs <b>$\\frac{n-1}{n}$</b></div></div>\n  <div class=\"glyph\"><div class=\"g\" style=\"color:#DB00FF\">*n&hellip;</div><div class=\"nm\">kaleidoscope · mirrors</div>\n    <p><span class=\"sym\">*</span> opens a mirror boundary; digits after it are corner points</p>\n    <div class=\"price\"><span class=\"sym\">*</span> costs <b>$1</b>, corner $n$ costs <b>$\\frac{n-1}{2n}$</b></div></div>\n  <div class=\"glyph\"><div class=\"g\" style=\"color:#8C0072\">&times;</div><div class=\"nm\">miracle · cross-cap</div>\n    <p>a glide reflection; sews in a cross-cap (written <span class=\"sym\">x</span> in SymmHub)</p><div class=\"price\">costs <b>$1</b></div></div>\n</div>\n\n<div class=\"prose\">\n<p>So <span class=\"sym\">*632</span> is a triangle kaleidoscope (the honeycomb group, p6m),\n<span class=\"sym\">442</span> spins without mirrors (p4), <span class=\"sym\">22&times;</span> is\ntwo half-turns and a miracle (pgg), and <span class=\"sym\">o</span> is nothing but translations (p1).</p>\n\n<div class=\"eyebrow syn\">Part II &nbsp;·&nbsp; The accounting</div>\n<h2>The Magic Theorem: every wallpaper costs exactly $2</h2>\n\n<p>Here is the piece of magic that Conway, Burgiel and Goodman-Strauss put at the center of\n<i>The Symmetries of Things</i> (and of its 2025 sequel, <i>The Magic Theorem</i>, finished by\nBurgiel and Goodman-Strauss after Conway's death in 2020). Give every symbol a price, as in the\ncards above. Then go shopping in the <em>Orbifold Shop</em> with two dollars in your pocket:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>spend <b>less than $2</b> and your group lives on the <b>sphere</b> — there are exactly 14 types (7 infinite families and 7 polyhedral groups);</li>\n<li>spend <b>exactly $2</b> and it lives in the <b>Euclidean plane</b> — precisely the 17 wallpaper groups;</li>\n<li>spend <b>more than $2</b> and it lives in the <b>hyperbolic plane</b> — infinitely many groups, the ones SymmHub draws.</li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>The magic is bookkeeping for the Gauss&ndash;Bonnet theorem. The <em>orbifold Euler\ncharacteristic</em> is the honest Euler characteristic of the folded scrap, with cone and corner\npoints counted fractionally:</p>\n\n$$\\chi_{\\mathrm{orb}} \\;=\\; 2 \\;-\\; \\underbrace{2\\,(\\#o) \\;-\\; (\\#\\times) \\;-\\; (\\#*)\n\\;-\\; \\sum_{\\text{cones}}\\Bigl(1-\\tfrac1n\\Bigr) \\;-\\; \\tfrac12\\sum_{\\text{corners}}\\Bigl(1-\\tfrac1m\\Bigr)}_{\\text{the bill}}\n\\;=\\; 2 - \\text{cost},$$\n\n<p>and Gauss&ndash;Bonnet says $\\int K\\,dA = 2\\pi\\chi_{\\mathrm{orb}}$: positive characteristic\nforces spherical geometry, zero forces flat, negative forces hyperbolic — with hyperbolic area\nexactly $2\\pi\\,|\\chi_{\\mathrm{orb}}|$. This exact formula, thresholds and all, is what runs in\nSymmHub every time you press Enter in the symbol box\n(<a href=\"https://github.com/SymmHub/SymmHub/blob/main/lib/orbilib/OrbifoldGeometrization.js\"><span class=\"kbd\">OrbifoldGeometrization.js</span></a>,\nfunction <span class=\"kbd\">hashOrbifoldString</span>).</p>\n</div>\n\n<div class=\"widget calc\">\n  <div class=\"wtitle\"><span class=\"dot\" style=\"background:var(--gold)\"></span>Interactive · the Orbifold Shop till</div>\n  <div style=\"font-family:ui-sans-serif,system-ui,sans-serif;font-size:14px;color:var(--graphite);margin-bottom:10px\">\n    Type an orbifold symbol — digits, <span class=\"sym\">*</span>, <span class=\"sym\">x</span>, <span class=\"sym\">o</span>;\n    parenthesize multi-digit orders like <span class=\"sym\">(12)</span>. The till itemizes the bill, computes\n    $\\chi_{\\mathrm{orb}}$, classifies the geometry, and counts the degrees of freedom SymmHub will let you drag.\n  </div>\n  <input id=\"symInput\" type=\"text\" value=\"3456\" spellcheck=\"false\" autocomplete=\"off\">\n  <div class=\"exrow\">\n    <button data-s=\"*632\">*632</button><button data-s=\"442\">442</button><button data-s=\"22x\">22x</button>\n    <button data-s=\"o\">o</button><button data-s=\"2223\">2223</button><button data-s=\"3456\">3456</button>\n    <button data-s=\"34x\">34x</button><button data-s=\"*34x\">*34x</button><button data-s=\"*237\">*237</button>\n    <button data-s=\"oo\">oo</button><button data-s=\"532\">532</button>\n  </div>\n  <div id=\"receipt\" class=\"receipt\"></div>\n  <div id=\"verdict\" class=\"verdict\"></div>\n  <div class=\"mcheck\">machine check: <span id=\"selfcheck\"></span></div>\n</div>\n\n<div class=\"prose\">\n<div class=\"note\"><b>Reading the receipt.</b> <span class=\"sym\">*237</span> is the cheapest possible\noverspend — $2\\tfrac1{84}$, so $\\chi=-\\tfrac1{84}$ — the smallest hyperbolic orbifold, whose group\nis the (2,3,7) triangle group of Klein's quartic. Escher's <i>Circle Limit IV</i> (angels and devils)\nis <span class=\"sym\">4*3</span>, $\\chi = -\\tfrac1{12}$. Every over-$2 symbol is a genuinely new\nuniverse of wallpaper; the notation is a catalogue of infinitely many hyperbolic worlds.</div>\n\n<div class=\"eyebrow prb\">Part III &nbsp;·&nbsp; The lost thesis</div>\n<h2>From a symbol to an actual tiling: Deaton's construction</h2>\n\n<p>The Magic Theorem tells you <em>which</em> geometry a symbol lives in. It does not tell you how\nto <em>draw</em> it. To render <span class=\"sym\">3456</span> you must produce an honest hyperbolic\npolygon — a fundamental domain — together with the M&ouml;bius transformations that glue its edges,\nand this is a real construction problem: the recipe is only sketched in Thurston's notes\n(<i>The Geometry and Topology of Three-Manifolds</i>, ch.&nbsp;13), via triangles that are allowed\nto have <em>imaginary angles</em>.</p>\n\n<p>The missing link is a thesis that barely exists in the record. In 1994 a Princeton undergraduate,\n<b>Adam Deaton</b>, wrote a senior thesis — Conway's era at Princeton; the source of the\nhalf-remembered &ldquo;Conway student's thesis&rdquo; story, though it was an undergraduate thesis,\nnot a master's — working out Thurston's sketch into an algorithm, together with a drawing program.\nNeither was ever published. Goodman-Strauss has noted that the algorithm lived on in Deaton's\n&ldquo;wonderful drawing program&rdquo; from the early 1990s while its details went undocumented —\nso he reconstructed the method himself. His reconstruction, in his own words &ldquo;digested&rdquo;\nfrom Thurston and Deaton, is exactly the engine in this repository: the header of\n<span class=\"kbd\">OrbifoldGeometrization.js</span> cites &ldquo;Adam Deaton's 1994 Princeton\nUniversity undergraduate thesis&rdquo; by name.</p>\n\n<p>The construction decomposes any hyperbolic orbifold into three species of <b>atoms</b> —\nmirror-bounded triangles (<i>sheets</i>, $*pqr$), doubled triangles with three cone-type features\n(<i>pillows</i>, $pqr$), and half-and-half <i>hats</i> ($p*q$) — cutting along two kinds of seams:\n<b>tubes</b> (cone-to-cone cuts) and <b>slices</b> (cone-to-mirror cuts). Each atom unfolds into a\ngeodesic polygon in the Poincar&eacute; disk by hyperbolic trigonometry (the generalized law of\ncosines handles the imaginary angles: a &ldquo;vertex&rdquo; with imaginary angle $i\\ell$ is really\na perpendicular geodesic edge of length $\\ell$), and the atoms are welded back together edge-to-edge\nby M&ouml;bius maps:</p>\n</div>\n\n<div class=\"pipe\">\n  <div class=\"stage\"><b>parse</b><span><span class=\"kbd\">hashOrbifoldString</span> — symbol → features, $\\chi_{\\mathrm{orb}}$, geometry</span></div>\n  <div class=\"arr\">→</div>\n  <div class=\"stage\"><b>normalize</b><span><span class=\"kbd\">hashOrbifold</span> — pair 2-fold points, open handles &amp; cross-caps, merge mirror circles</span></div>\n  <div class=\"arr\">→</div>\n  <div class=\"stage\"><b>atomize</b><span><span class=\"kbd\">atomizeOrbifold</span> — cut along tubes &amp; slices into sheets / pillows / hats</span></div>\n  <div class=\"arr\">→</div>\n  <div class=\"stage\"><b>unfold</b><span><span class=\"kbd\">unfoldAtom</span> — turtle geometry walks each atom out as a disk polygon</span></div>\n  <div class=\"arr\">→</div>\n  <div class=\"stage\"><b>assemble</b><span><span class=\"kbd\">assembleFundamentalDomain</span> — weld atoms along seams (twists applied here)</span></div>\n  <div class=\"arr\">→</div>\n  <div class=\"stage\"><b>generate</b><span><span class=\"kbd\">produceGenerators</span> — one inversion-circle list per edge → the group, packed for the GPU</span></div>\n</div>\n\n<div class=\"prose\">\n\n<div class=\"eyebrow phy\">Part IV &nbsp;·&nbsp; The drags</div>\n<h2>What you are really dragging: Teichm&uuml;ller space</h2>\n\n<p>Here is the payoff. A spherical or Euclidean group is rigid up to scale: <span class=\"sym\">*632</span>\nis the honeycomb, end of story. A <em>hyperbolic</em> orbifold is different — the same group signature\nadmits a continuous family of genuinely distinct hyperbolic shapes. Thurston (Cor.&nbsp;13.3.7) computes\nthe dimension of that family, its <b>Teichm&uuml;ller space</b>:</p>\n\n$$\\dim \\mathcal{T}(O) \\;=\\; -3\\,\\chi(X_O) \\;+\\; 2k \\;+\\; l,$$\n\n<p>where $\\chi(X_O)$ is the ordinary Euler characteristic of the underlying surface, $k$ counts cone\npoints and $l$ counts corner reflectors. And his proof is a recipe: cut the orbifold along disjoint\ngeodesics into pants-like primitive pieces; then <em>the lengths of the cuts, plus a twist angle for\neach gluing along a closed geodesic, are global coordinates</em>. These are the <b>Fenchel&ndash;Nielsen\ncoordinates</b> of the orbifold.</p>\n\n<p>Now look at what SymmHub puts in the settings panel when you type <span class=\"sym\">

# TLDR **The dragging works again — in both apps.** I found why it died, fixed it in the old Symmetry.html app, added true click-and-drag (it was originally hover+wheel only), ported the whole interaction into the new SymPix app, and wrote the tutorial page you asked for, ready to link on GitHub Pages: [tutorials/orbifold-notation.html](tutorials/orbifold-notation.html) (also linked from the site's [index.html](index.html)). ## What was actually broken Chaim Goodman-Strauss's interactive editor (`SymmetryUIController`, designed in his Nov-2019 code, committed Feb 2025) worked as: hover a fundamental-domain edge → it highlights → wheel changes its length (shift+wheel: twist) → `setShift()` re-anchors the view so the grabbed point stays put. Three things killed it: 1. **A navigator refactor removed the API it relied on.** `setShift` did `[...this.transform.transforms, ...]`, but `InversiveNavigator` now stores its transform in `config.inversive.itrans` — every wheel gesture threw `TypeError: transforms is not iterable` (I reproduced it live with a stack trace). Fixed via `get/setInversiveTransform()`, plus I re-enabled the `iGetFactorizationU4` compaction so the transform list stays bounded instead of growing forever. 2. **The feature was invisible**: the domain overlay defaulted off, and the Space toggle crashed on a controller (`config.controllers.domain`) that no longer exists. Now edges show by default and Space toggles safely. 3. **The new SymPix app never wired it at all** — `Group_Orbifold` stubbed the controller with no-ops. I wrote [lib/orbilib/OrbifoldUITool.js](lib/orbilib/OrbifoldUITool.js) (a modernized port) and hooked it into `SymRenderer`'s tool chain ahead of the navigator. There's a **show edges** checkbox in *symmetry → group params*. I also merged Chaim's own unmerged bug-fix branch `upstream/temp12626` ("fixed a lot of buggy behavior" — texture/crown transforms, the likely Windows browser-killer along with per-frame console.log floods, now silenced), and an adversarial review pass over the diff surfaced 11 real defects (shift+wheel eaten by a keydown reset, stale-hover grabs, Euclidean-switch crash storm, right-click starting drags, glide-race with the pan animation…) — all fixed and re-verified in the browser. Everything is uncommitted on `main` (local `main` was also fast-forwarded to upstream), ready for you to review and commit. ## What the drags *are*, mathematically A hyperbolic orbifold symbol with negative orbifold Euler characteristic isn't rigid — it has a **Teichmüller space** of genuinely different hyperbolic shapes, of dimension `−3χ(X) + 2·(cone points) + (corner reflectors)` (Thurston, Cor. 13.3.7). The code computes this as `−6 + 6·o + 3·x + 2·cones + 3·* + corners`. The sliders/drags are **Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates**: `tube_1_l` is the hyperbolic length of a pants-decomposition seam, `tube_1_t` is the twist — how far one side slides along the seam before gluing. Dragging an edge is literally walking through the moduli space of that symmetry group. Mirror-anchored cuts (`slice`, `band`) lose their twist because the gluing must carry mirror to mirror — which is why `*34x` has two lengths and no twist. ## The history (with one correction to the story) Thurston invented orbifolds; the notation is Conway's (~1990), which he described as an elegant form of Macbeath's 1967 signature; Conway–Huson 2002 and *The Symmetries of Things* (2008, Conway–Burgiel–**Goodman-Strauss**) made it canonical, with the **Magic Theorem**: price the symbols (o=$2, n=(n−1)/n, \*=×=$1, corner n=(n−1)/2n) — under $2 spherical, exactly $2 the 17 wallpapers, over $2 hyperbolic. The "master's thesis" you remembered is real but was an **undergraduate senior thesis: Adam Deaton, Princeton 1994** (Conway's Princeton era) — it worked Thurston's sketch into an algorithm plus a drawing program, was never published, and Goodman-Strauss reconstructed ("digested") it; his `OrbifoldGeometrization.js` cites it by name and implements exactly its atoms pipeline (parse → atomize into sheets/pillows/hats → unfold with imaginary-angle trigonometry → weld with Möbius maps). Git archaeology: Chaim authored 97 commits here — the geometrization engine, `WallPaperGroup_General`, the interaction model and the crown/texture machinery are his line of work; the GL rendering framework is Vladimir's. All of this, with sources, the interactive "Orbifold Shop till" (it self-checks χ(\*237)=−1/84 etc. on load), the edge-color legend, and the live app embedded, is in the tutorial. Once pushed to `upstream/main` it will be at `https://symmhub.github.io/SymmHub/tutorials/orbifold-notation.html`. **Try it now**: the local server is running — [sympix_orbifold.html](http://localhost:8932/apps/sympic/sympix_orbifold.html) → hover the orange/blue arcs until one glows yellow, then drag; shift+drag twists; `*237` highlights nothing because triangle groups are rigid, exactly as the dimension formula says.

 "content": "Resurrects Chaim Goodman-Strauss's interactive editing of orbifold parameters — hover a fundamental-domain edge, it highlights, and you change its length/twist directly on the image — which had been broken in the legacy app and never wired into the new SymPix app. Adds true click-and-drag on top of the original wheel interaction, and a tutorial page explaining the mathematics.\n\n## Why it was broken\n\n- `SymmetryUIController.setShift()` still used `navigator.transforms`, removed in the `InversiveNavigator` refactor (`config.inversive.itrans` now) — every wheel gesture threw `TypeError: this.transform.transforms is not iterable`, killing the view re-anchoring.\n- The domain overlay defaulted off and the Space toggle crashed on `config.controllers.domain`, which no longer exists — so the feature was invisible even where it half-worked.\n- The SymPix app's `Group_Orbifold` adapter stubbed the controller with no-ops, and `SymRenderer` never forwarded events or overlay drawing to the group maker.\n\n## What this PR does\n\n**Legacy app** (`apps/orbifold/Symmetry.html`)\n- Fixes `setShift()` to use `get/setInversiveTransform()` and re-enables the `iGetFactorizationU4` compaction so the navigator transform list stays bounded.\n- Adds drag-to-edit: press on a highlighted edge and drag to change its length; shift-drag (or shift-wheel) changes the twist. The grabbed point stays anchored under the cursor while the domain reshapes.\n- Fixes: Space toggle, interior-edge indexing in `onWheel`, keydown resetting the hover state (shift+wheel twist never worked without moving the mouse), stale `FDPoints` after switching to a Euclidean/spherical symbol (event-handler exception storm), texture-control-point priority over edge grabbing, primary-button filter, race with a still-gliding pan animation, `needsShiftQ` never being reset.\n- Shows the domain edges by default; merges the unmerged `temp12626` PatternTextures fixes (\"fixed a lot of buggy behavior\") and gates the per-frame `console.log` floods behind the debug flag.\n\n**SymPix app** (`apps/sympic/sympix_orbifold.html`)\n- New `lib/orbilib/OrbifoldUITool.js` — a port of the controller to the SymRenderer pipeline (`e.isConsumed` protocol; draws the color-coded fundamental-domain edges on the 2D overlay; hover/drag/wheel; same `setShift` re-anchoring).\n- `Group_Orbifold.createUITool()` replaces the no-op `symmetryUI` stub and adds a **show edges** checkbox under *symmetry → group params* (not serialized — presets are unaffected).\n- `SymRenderer` runs the group maker's UI tool ahead of the navigator in move-tool mode (consuming `pointerdown` on an edge so the `AnimatedPointer` never starts panning) and renders it each frame. Group makers without `createUITool` are untouched; the other SymPix/SymSim apps behave exactly as before.\n\n**Tutorial** — `tutorials/orbifold-notation.html` (\"Two Dollars of Symmetry\", linked from `index.html`): Conway's orbifold notation and its history (Macbeath → Thurston → Conway → Conway–Burgiel–Goodman-Strauss), the Magic Theorem with an interactive cost calculator that self-checks against the same Euler-characteristic formula as `OrbifoldGeometrization.js`, the Deaton-1994 atoms geometrization pipeline the engine implements, and the Teichmüller/Fenchel–Nielsen meaning of the length/twist drags — with the live SymPix app embedded.\n\n## Testing\n\nVerified interactively in a browser (both apps, served locally): hover highlight + grab cursor; drag/wheel/shift variants change `conePair_1_l`, `tube_1_l/t`, `cap_1_l` with the settings panel updating live; view re-anchoring keeps the grabbed point fixed with the transform list bounded; pan/zoom/texture drag still work away from edges; preset loading and group-type switching recreate the tool; Euclidean/spherical symbols disable the overlay cleanly; `sympix_wp.html` (non-orbifold) unaffected. All changed files pass `node --check`. An adversarial review pass over the diff surfaced 11 defects (keydown/hover reset, stale-press grabs, zero-coordinate throw at the canvas edge, glide race, …) — all fixed and re-verified.\n\nKnown limitations (documented in `OrbifoldUITool.js`): the overlay ignores a non-identity *group transform* (identity is the default), and the re-anchoring is only approximate after ctrl/shift elliptic–hyperbolic navigation gestures.\n\n🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)\n"

I'm looking at a table of transformation rules in orbifold notation that shows how different pattern sequences rewrite into simplified forms, with rules involving asterisks, x's, o's, and numbers that collapse into infinity symbols.

Then there's a catalog of twelve atomic building blocks—sheets, pillows, and pillowcases (which the text notes are equivalent to what other sources call "hats")—and a procedure for cutting pillows in half to generate new configurations with specific parameter substitutions.

In the Teichmüller space section, I'm trying to understand how twist parameters arise specifically when cutting annulus neighborhoods into two pieces, and the text indicates this happens only with certain rules, though I'm catching myself mid-thought as I reread the exact conditions. The implementation chapter describes how lafite computes the hyperbolic structure through gluing diagrams and connection graphs, with a key insight about semigroup versus group generators requiring different numbers of multiplications to close. What really stands out is that lafite enabled interactive parameter adjustment—users could drag length and twist values and watch the hyperbolic structure recalculate smoothly in real-time on 1990s workstations, which was the original interactive visualization system. The codebase itself spans over 4000 lines of C across multiple modules for decomposition, hyperbolic calculations, and group elements.

The gallery chapter showcases replicated Escher designs with specific notation for their symmetry groups—Circle Limit I uses 2*23, Circle Limit III uses 334 (or 22222 when counting colors)—and includes several gallery examples, notably the 23x pattern with glide-reflection feet that matches the red preset in SymmHub, plus an ∞∞∞ configuration with three infinite-order cone points that Escher never used in his Circle Limit series.

I'm noting the bibliography references for this work on three-dimensional geometry and topology, pulling from Thurston's foundational text along with Conway's work on orbifold notation and surface groups, plus Schattschneider's visual exploration of symmetry.

Looking at the document structure, I've traced through pages 1-24 and then 25-40, confirming there's no advisor acknowledgment listed—the thesis moves directly from the declaration into the content. The work cites Conway's forthcoming publications and sits within the Princeton mathematical community around Conway and Thurston's research.

The actual thesis is Adam A. Deaton's 1993 BA senior thesis titled "Hyperbolic Orbifolds and Patterns," written in C as a program called lafite with roughly 4000 lines of code. Deaton's approach introduces boundary symbols through cuts and expresses nine different cut types as rewrite rules operating on the notation itself.

The core mathematical objects are twelve atoms—sheets, pillows, and pillowcases (which CGS later renamed to hats)—that get halved into generalized triangles with imaginary angles, solved within the hyperboloid model. The twists arise specifically from three sources: cuts around handles, cuts between order-2 cone points, and cuts around pairs of cone points, which maps directly onto CGS's later twistKeys structure. Each twist is measured relative to the circular cut's length as a fractional parameter in ℝ, and the Teichmüller space decomposes as ℝⁿ where n counts the lengths and twists. Notably, lafite already had interactive parameter editing built in, allowing the picture to shift smoothly as values change.

The gallery spans examples like the Escher-like 644, Circle Limit I and III with their respective symmetry signatures, the "almost Euclidean" 245 (pillow cut in half with red/blue coloring), and special cases like 23* with no real Euclidean analogue, 23x as a glide-reflection motif that's literally the preset in SymmHub today, and 23∞ for flower bouquets. The bibliography includes Conway's forthcoming "ZIP Up Your Surfaces" and Schattschneider's Visions of Symmetry. I need to correct the year in Part III—the code comment says 1994 but the thesis is actually from 1993—and note that the advisor identity isn't stated in the document.

For the tutorial update, I'm rewriting Part III to fix the year to 1993, describe Deaton's actual method in his own structure (nine cuts as rewrite rules feeding into twelve atoms, halving into generalized triangles, solving via hyperboloid model, building the connection graph and generators with interactivity from the start), and mention that the thesis is now scanned from Princeton's Mudd Library. I'll also note the pillowcases-to-hats renaming in the code. For the warm-up section on rigid worlds, I'm cataloging the smallest hyperbolic orbifolds like *237 and *238, plus Deaton's "almost Euclidean" pillow (245) where I'm verifying the Euler characteristic works out to −1/20, then carefully distinguishing between rigid triangle groups and those with parameters to avoid confusion. Checking whether 4*3 gives Circle Limit IV symmetry with rigid constraints, then moving through *2345 as a slice family and 2*23 as Circle Limit I symmetry, before considering Euler characteristic to filter out spherical and Euclidean cases, and finally examining families with both length and twist parameters like 2223 and 3456. Continuing with the band structure—two kaleidoscopes form one band, and I need to think about how corner pairs work when adjacent 2s appear on the same kaleidoscope. I'm also considering not over-specifying slider names and instead letting the dimension speak for itself. Looking at a few more cases like *x with χ=0, *22x, and o* to understand the pattern. Then I want to examine some classic Escher corner examples across different crystallographic groups, and finally stress-test with larger moduli like repeated 2s and 3s. I'm setting up interaction experiments to test how the shift anchoring works when grabbing points, how twist wrapping behaves across the ±0.5 range, and verifying that the area invariant 2π|χ| holds constant as shapes deform. For the reference table, each entry needs the symbol, exact Euler characteristic, dimension, instructions for what to manipulate, and what visual behavior to expect. I'm noting that presets exist for a few cases like 23x, 345, and *3333 that can be linked via hash, while others require manual symbol entry—and I should flag that the parser handles parenthesized notation like (12) but doesn't support infinity symbols the way Deaton's examples do.

Now I'm spot-checking my dimension and χ calculations against the formula to make sure everything's consistent: the o3 case gives χ = −2/3 with dimension 2, o2 matches Deaton's −1/2 with dimension 2, the oo orbifold (genus 2) yields χ = −2 and dimension 6 which satisfies the genus formula 6g−6, o* works out to χ = −1 and dimension 3, and the five-cone case 22222 produces χ = −1/2 with dimension 4 matching what the execution verified earlier. Now checking some specific orbifold cases: the (2,2,∞) case isn't supported, but (6,3,4) gives χ=−1/4 with dimension 0, confirming it's rigid. to)</div>\n\n<div class=\"hero prose\" style=\"max-width:880px\">\n  <div class=\"eyebrow ink\" style=\"margin-top:0\">SymmHub &nbsp;·&nbsp; field guide &nbsp;·&nbsp; type the symbol, hover an edge, drag</div>\n  <h1>A Field Guide of Orbifold Experiments</h1>\n  <p class=\"sub\">Thirty-plus symmetry groups worth visiting, from rigid triangle worlds to\n  six-dimensional moduli monsters — each with its Euler characteristic $\\chi$, the number of\n  parameters you can drag, and what to watch while you drag them. Work with the app below, or open\n  it <a href=\"../apps/sympic/sympix_orbifold.html\" target=\"_blank\">in its own tab</a>.</p>\n</div>\n\n<figure>\n  <iframe class=\"app\" src=\"../apps/sympic/sympix_orbifold.html#%7B%22preset%22%3A%22presets%2Forbifold%2Fpar-26-05-11-16-54-33-010.json%22%7D\"\n    title=\"SymPix orbifold app\" loading=\"lazy\"></iframe>\n  <figcaption>Type any symbol from the tables into <i>settings → symmetry → group params → orbifold\n  symbol</i> and press Enter. Hover a colored arc until it glows yellow; <b>drag</b> to change its\n  length, <b>shift-drag</b> (or shift-wheel) to twist. Multi-digit orders need parentheses:\n  <span class=\"sym\">(12)</span>. The legacy app works too: <a href=\"../apps/orbifold/Symmetry.html\" target=\"_blank\">Symmetry.html</a>\n  (Space toggles the edge overlay there).</figcaption>\n  <div class=\"legend\">\n    <span><span class=\"swatch\" style=\"background:#0000E1\"></span>conePair</span>\n    <span><span class=\"swatch\" style=\"background:#EBAD00\"></span>tube / slice / band</span>\n    <span><span class=\"swatch\" style=\"background:#0000FF\"></span>handle</span>\n    <span><span class=\"swatch\" style=\"background:#8C0072\"></span>cap</span>\n    <span><span class=\"swatch\" style=\"background:#DB0000\"></span>fold / cornerPair</span>\n    <span><span class=\"swatch\" style=\"background:#92C4DD\"></span>cuttingEdge (not draggable)</span>\n    <span><span class=\"swatch\" style=\"background:#FFFF00;border:1px solid #ccc\"></span>active</span>\n  </div>\n</figure>\n\n<div class=\"prose\">\n<p>Every entry lists the exact orbifold Euler characteristic $\\chi$ (cost $= 2-\\chi$; hyperbolic\narea $=2\\pi|\\chi|$) and <b>dim</b>, the dimension of the Teichm&uuml;ller space — the number of\nlength/twist sliders SymmHub creates. A tiny script at the bottom of this page recomputes every\n$\\chi$ and every dim from the symbol on each load and flags any row I got wrong, so the tables\ncannot silently rot.</p>\n\n<div class=\"eyebrow phy\">I &nbsp;·&nbsp; Rigid worlds (dim 0)</div>\n<h2>Warm-ups: nothing to drag, everything to see</h2>\n<p>Triangle groups — three cone points ($pqr$) or a three-cornered kaleidoscope ($*pqr$) — have no\nmoduli at all: the trigonometry pins every length. Hover all you like; nothing lights up. These\ncalibrate your eye for what &ldquo;rigid&rdquo; looks like, and they contain the most famous\nhyperbolic groups.</p>\n</div>\n\n<div class=\"tablewrap\"><table class=\"pins\">\n<tr><th>symbol</th><th>χ</th><th>dim</th><th>what it is &amp; what to notice</th></tr>\n<tr class=\"gold\"><td class=\"c\"><span class=\"sym\" data-sym=\"*237\" data-chi=\"-1/84\" data-dim=\"0\">*237</span></td><td class=\"c\">−1/84</td><td class=\"c\">0</td>\n  <td>The cheapest possible overspend — the smallest hyperbolic orbifold, mirror triangle of the (2,3,7) group.\n  Its area $2\\pi/84$ is the floor for all hyperbolic orbifolds; the Klein quartic is tiled by 336 copies of it.\n  Note how tiny the fundamental triangle is on screen.</td></tr>\n<tr><td class=\"c\"><span class=\"sym\" data-sym=\"237\" data-chi=\"-1/42\" data-dim=\"0\">237</span></td><td class=\"c\">−1/42</td><td class=\"c\">0</td>\n  <td>The same world without mirrors: the orientation-preserving (2,3,7) <i>Hurwitz</i> group — the symmetry\n  budget behind surfaces with the maximum possible 84(g−1) automorphisms. A doubled *237.</td></tr>\n<tr><td class=\"c\"><span class=\"sym\" data-sym=\"*238\" data-chi=\"-1/24\" data-dim=\"0\">*238</span></td><td class=\"c\">−1/24</td><td class=\"c\">0</td>\n  <td>The octagonal kaleidoscope: regular hyperbolic octagons come from here. Compare its triangle size with *237's.</td></tr>\n<tr><td class=\"c\"><span class=\"sym\" data-sym=\"245\" data-chi=\"-1/20\" data-dim=\"0\">245</span></td><td class=\"c\">−1/20</td><td class=\"c\">0</td>\n  <td>Deaton's opening gallery piece (1993): an &ldquo;almost Euclidean&rdquo; three-cornered pillow — χ is barely\n  below zero, so the tiling looks nearly flat near the center and only crushes toward the rim far out.</td></tr>\n<tr><td class=\"c\"><span class=\"sym\" data-sym=\"344\" data-chi=\"-1/6\" data-dim=\"0\">344</span></td><td class=\"c\">−1/6</td><td class=\"c\">0</td>\n  <td>Three cone points, no mirrors. Watch the three gyration centers in the pattern: 3-fold and two 4-folds.</td></tr>\n<tr><td class=\"c\"><span class=\"sym\" data-sym=\"644\" data-chi=\"-1/3\" data-dim=\"0\">644</span></td><td class=\"c\">−1/3</td><td class=\"c\">0</td>\n  <td>The group of the two Escher-style pictures opening Deaton's thesis — his stand-in for the <i>Circle Limit</i>\n  construction. A good one for the pattern tool: strong 6-fold center.</td></tr>\n<tr><td class=\"c\"><span class=\"sym\" data-sym=\"*2345\" data-chi=\"-43/120\" data-dim=\"1\">*2345</span></td><td class=\"c\">−43/120</td><td class=\"c\">1</td>\n  <td>Four corners on one mirror circle — the first kaleidoscope with a modulus. Deaton's own worked\n  example of a length parameter: his cut *2345 → *23∞ + *∞45. Drag the orange <span class=\"kbd\">slice</span> seam\n  and watch a four-cornered hall of mirrors reshape. (In this row as a bridge to Part II.)</td></tr>\n</table></div>\n\n<div class=\"prose\">\n<div class=\"eyebrow syn\">II &nbsp;·&nbsp; One knob (dim 1)</div>\n<h2>Single-parameter families: pure lengths</h2>\n<p>One slider, no twist — every one of these is a single geodesic length, frozen against twisting\nby a mirror or by cross-cap symmetry. Drag slowly and watch the <em>area stay exactly constant</em>\n(it is $2\\pi|\\chi|$, a topological invariant!) while the proportions redistribute.</p>\n</div>\n\n<div class=\"tablewrap\"><table class=\"pins\">\n<tr><th>symbol</th><th>χ</th><th>dim</th><th>what it is &amp; what to notice</th></tr>\n<tr class=\"gold\"><td class=\"c\"><span class=\"sym\" data-sym=\"23x\" data-chi=\"-1/6\" data-dim=\"1\">23x</span></td><td class=\"c\">−1/6</td><td class=\"c\">1</td>\n  <td>The app's default preset, and a star of Deaton's gallery: he drew walking feet along the\n  <span class=\"kbd\">cap</span> edge to make the hyperbolic glide-reflection visible — footprints\n  alternate left/right along the purple arc. Drag the cap and watch the glide axis stretch.</td></tr>\n<tr><td class=\"c\"><span class=\"sym\" data-sym=\"34x\" data-chi=\"-5/12\" data-dim=\"1\">34x</span></td><td class=\"c\">−5/12</td><td class=\"c\">1</td>\n  <td>A 3-fold, a 4-fold, and a miracle. One purple <span class=\"kbd\">cap_1_l</span> edge; its glide is half its length.</td></tr>\n<tr><td class=\"c\"><span class=\"sym\" data-sym=\"23*\" data-chi=\"-1/6\" data-dim=\"1\">23*</span></td><td class=\"c\">−1/6</td><td class=\"c\">1</td>\n  <td>Deaton: &ldquo;no real Euclidean analogue&rdquo; — gyrations <em>plus</em> a plain mirror circle with no corners.\n  Same χ as 23x, utterly different geometry: compare them! The slider is the <span class=\"kbd\">slice</span> from\n  the cones to the mirror.</td></tr>\n<tr><td class=\"c\"><span class=\"sym\" data-sym=\"2*23\" data-chi=\"-1/12\" data-dim=\"1\">2*23</span></td><td class=\"c\">−1/12</td><td class=\"c\">1</td>\n  <td>Escher's <i>Circle Limit I</i> has exactly this symmetry (per Deaton's gallery notes). One 2-fold gyration\n  off the mirror, corners 2 and 3 on it.</td></tr>\n<tr><td class=\"c\"><span class=\"sym\" data-sym=\"4*3\" data-chi=\"-1/12\" data-dim=\"0\">4*3</span></td><td class=\"c\">−1/12</td><td class=\"c\">0</td>\n  <td><i>Circle Limit IV</i> (angels &amp; devils), per Conway–Huson. Same price as 2*23, but rigid — a\n  reminder that χ alone does not decide whether you get a knob.</td></tr>\n<tr><td class=\"c\"><span class=\"sym\" data-sym=\"*3333\" data-chi=\"-1/3\" data-dim=\"1\">*3333</span></td><td class=\"c\">−1/3</td><td class=\"c\">1</td>\n  <td>Four 3-fold corners on one mirror — the hyperbolic cousin of the Euclidean *333. Ships as a preset.\n  Drag the slice: the four corner chambers trade area.</td></tr>\n<tr><td class=\"c\"><span class=\"sym\" data-sym=\"*22222\" data-chi=\"-1/4\" data-dim=\"2\">*22222</span></td><td class=\"c\">−1/4</td><td class=\"c\">2</td>\n  <td>Five right-angled corners — the right-angled hyperbolic pentagon! Adjacent 2-fold corners pair up\n  (<span class=\"kbd\">cornerPair</span>, red), giving two draggable lengths. The all-right-angle pentagon\n  is the standard first example of hyperbolic flexibility.</td></tr>\n</table></div>\n\n<div class=\"prose\">\n<div class=\"eyebrow prb\">III &nbsp;·&nbsp; Length + twist (Fenchel–Nielsen proper)</div>\n<h2>Seams you can slide: the twistable families</h2>\n<p>Deaton proved the twist appears in exactly three situations — a cut around a <b>handle</b>,\nbetween two <b>order-2 cone points</b>, or around a <b>pair of cones</b> — and those are precisely\nthe code's <span class=\"kbd\">twistKeys</span>. Here the drag is two-dimensional: plain drag changes\nthe seam's length, <b>shift-drag slides the two sides against each other</b>. The twist wraps\naround at ±½: watch the pattern shear, snap, and return.</p>\n</div>\n\n<div class=\"tablewrap\"><table class=\"pins\">\n<tr><th>symbol</th><th>χ</th><th>dim</th><th>what it is &amp; what to notice</th></tr>\n<tr class=\"gold\"><td class=\"c\"><span class=\"sym\" data-sym=\"2223\" data-chi=\"-1/6\" data-dim=\"2\">2223</span></td><td class=\"c\">−1/6</td><td class=\"c\">2</td>\n  <td>The classic first flexible orbifold: two of the 2-fold cones pair into a dark-blue\n  <span class=\"kbd\">conePair</span> edge. Drag = the pair separates or approaches; shift-drag = the\n  half-turn center slides along the edge. Watch distant copies of the pattern whirl as you twist.</td></tr>\n<tr><td class=\"c\"><span class=\"sym\" data-sym=\"3456\" data-chi=\"-21/20\" data-dim=\"2\">3456</span></td><td class=\"c\">−21/20</td><td class=\"c\">2</td>\n  <td>Four cones of four different orders — the atomizer cuts them into two pillows joined by an\n  orange <span class=\"kbd\">tube</span>: a genuine pair-of-pants seam. This is the textbook\n  Fenchel–Nielsen picture, live.</td></tr>\n<tr><td class=\"c\"><span class=\"sym\" data-sym=\"o2\" data-chi=\"-1/2\" data-dim=\"2\">o2</span></td><td class=\"c\">−1/2</td><td class=\"c\">2</td>\n  <td>Deaton's own twisting demo (his Figure 3.5): a handle plus one 2-fold cone. His rule\n  o → ∞<sub>ℓ</sub>∞<sub>ℓ</sub> makes the handle a circular cut with length <em>and</em> twist —\n  reproduce his figure by shift-dragging the blue <span class=\"kbd\">handle</span> edge through a full wrap.</td></tr>\n<tr><td class=\"c\"><span class=\"sym\" data-sym=\"o3\" data-chi=\"-2/3\" data-dim=\"2\">o3</span></td><td class=\"c\">−2/3</td><td class=\"c\">2</td>\n  <td>The first hyperbolic example in Deaton's thesis (his Figure 2.3, drawn as a torus with one cone\n  point): hyperbolic &ldquo;stack bond&rdquo; brickwork. The two arrow-translations of the brick wall\n  become the handle gluing you are dragging.</td></tr>\n<tr><td class=\"c\"><span class=\"sym\" data-sym=\"2224\" data-chi=\"-1/4\" data-dim=\"2\">2224</span></td><td class=\"c\">−1/4</td><td class=\"c\">2</td>\n  <td>Like 2223 but with a 4-fold anchor: a conePair plus leftovers. Compare how the twist feels\n  against 2223 — the higher-order cone stiffens the picture.</td></tr>\n<tr><td class=\"c\"><span class=\"sym\" data-sym=\"22*2\" data-chi=\"-1/4\" data-dim=\"2\">22*2</span></td><td class=\"c\">−1/4</td><td class=\"c\">2</td>\n  <td>Two free 2-fold cones (they pair up — twistable!) plus a mirror with one corner. A rare\n  mix: one twistable conePair seam <em>and</em> mirror-frozen structure in the same picture.</td></tr>\n</table></div>\n\n<div class=\"prose\">\n<div class=\"eyebrow phy\">IV &nbsp;·&nbsp; Big moduli (dim ≥ 3)</div>\n<h2>Multi-dimensional Teichm&uuml;ller spaces</h2>\n<p>Now several edges highlight, each an independent coordinate. Try &ldquo;playing chords&rdquo;:\nset one length long, another short, twist a third — every combination is a genuinely different\nhyperbolic world with the same group signature. The area still never budges.</p>\n</div>\n\n<div class=\"tablewrap\"><table class=\"pins\">\n<tr><th>symbol</th><th>χ</th><th>dim</th><th>what it is &amp; what to notice</th></tr>\n<tr><td class=\"c\"><span class=\"sym\" data-sym=\"o*\" data-chi=\"-1\" data-dim=\"3\">o*</span></td><td class=\"c\">−1</td><td class=\"c\">3</td>\n  <td>A handle and a bare mirror circle: handle length + twist, plus the band to the mirror. Non-orientable\n  meets orientable plumbing in one symbol.</td></tr>\n<tr class=\"gold\"><td class=\"c\"><span class=\"sym\" data-sym=\"22222\" data-chi=\"-1/2\" data-dim=\"4\">22222</span></td><td class=\"c\">−1/2</td><td class=\"c\">4</td>\n  <td>Five half-turns: two conePairs (each with length + twist) and a spare cone. Four sliders. Set the\n  two pair-lengths very unequal, then twist one — hyperbolic crystallography as a musical instrument.</td></tr>\n<tr><td class=\"c\"><span class=\"sym\" data-sym=\"33333\" data-chi=\"-4/3\" data-dim=\"4\">33333</span></td><td class=\"c\">−4/3</td><td class=\"c\">4</td>\n  <td>Five 3-folds: no 2-fold pairing available, so the atomizer carves it with <span class=\"kbd\">tube</span>s —\n  two tubes, each length + twist. I'm also updating the tutorial sections, particularly Part III and Part IV on twist provenance, along with the references.

Done — everything verified against the real thesis, expanded, deployed, and pushed to [PR #11](https://github.com/SymmHub/SymmHub/pull/11). ## What the thesis actually says (and what I corrected) **Adam A. Deaton, *Hyperbolic Orbifolds and Patterns*, Princeton senior thesis, 1993** — several details of the received story needed fixing: - **The year is 1993** (title page: "Princeton, 1993"). The SymmHub code comment says 1994, your filename says 1992 — both off by a year. - **The program has a name: *lafite*** — over 4,000 lines of C, and the thesis states it already let the user *change the length and twist parameters interactively, recalculating the hyperbolic structure on the fly* — smoothly, on a 1993 workstation. The drag you asked me to resurrect is a direct descendant of a 1993 feature. - **The method is even closer to the SymmHub code than expected**: nine cut types expressed as *rewrite rules on the notation itself* (e.g. `o → ∞ℓ∞ℓ`), leaving exactly **twelve atoms** — sheets, pillows, and "**pillowcases**" (which Goodman-Strauss's code renamed *hats*). Best of all: Deaton proves twists arise from exactly three cuts — around a handle, between order-2 cones, around a cone pair — which is **one-for-one the code's `twistKeys = [handle, conePair, tube]`**. - Escher pedigrees from his gallery: *Circle Limit I* = `2*23`, *Circle Limit III* = `334` (or `22222` counting colors); his own demos were `644`, `245`, `23*`, `23x` (the walking-feet glide-reflection picture — today literally SymmHub's default preset), and `o2` for twisting. - The thesis **names no advisor**, so the tutorial doesn't claim one — it notes only the Conway/Thurston Princeton orbit (it cites Conway's then-unpublished "ZIP Up Your Surfaces" and Thurston's then-forthcoming book). ## The expanded experiments — a separate page, as you suggested **https://yaroslavvb.github.io/SymmHub/tutorials/orbifold-experiments.html** "A Field Guide of Orbifold Experiments": **32 symbols in 6 sections** — rigid warm-ups (`*237`, Hurwitz `237`, Deaton's `245`), one-knob families (`23x`, `2*23`, the right-angled pentagon `*22222`), true Fenchel–Nielsen seams to twist (`2223`, `3456`, Deaton's `o2`/`o3`), big moduli up to dim 8 (genus-2 `oo` with its full 6-dimensional Teichmüller space), the Escher/Deaton pedigree table, instructive refusals (teardrops, Euclidean/spherical, the unsupported `∞`), and experiments about the interaction itself (the anchor, constant area under Gauss–Bonnet, twist wrap-around, degeneration at the slider clamps). Every row lists exact χ and moduli count, **recomputed from the symbol by an in-page self-check on every load** — which earned its keep immediately: it caught two arithmetic errors of mine (χ(`334`)=−1/12, χ(`*238`)=−1/48) and a fraction-formatter bug before anything shipped. The main tutorial got the matching updates (Part III rewritten around *lafite* and the rewrite-rule pipeline, the twist-provenance paragraph in Part IV, corrected references and correction notes) and links to the guide: **https://yaroslavvb.github.io/SymmHub/tutorials/orbifold-notation.html**. Both pages are live on your fork's Pages and in the PR. One caution: the scan carries a Princeton University Archives rights statement requiring permission before republishing — so I cited the thesis in the tutorial but did **not** commit the PDF to the repo; best to keep it that way unless you clear it with the Mudd Library.

    return myself;

    // ── Initialisation ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    function init() {
        window.addEventListener('hashchange', onHashChange);
        if (mSamplesData) {
            onShowSamples();
            mSamplesSelector.addItems(mSamplesData);
        }
        try {
            if (window.localStorage.getItem('docFileDialog_visible') === 'true') {
                onShowDocuments();
            }
        } catch (e) {
            console.warn('localStorage error in SymDocumentManager init:', e);
        }
    }

    function createInitialDocument() {
        mCurrentDocument = mDocHandler.createDocument({
            appInfo:        mAppInfo,
            params:         mParams,
            thumbMaker:     getThumbMaker(),
            rendererConfig: mRendererConfig,
        });
        return mCurrentDocument;
    }

    // ── Hash navigation ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    function onHashChange() {
        let opt = getHashParams();
        if(DEBUG)console.log(`${MYNAME}.onHashChange()`, opt);
        if(opt.preset) readParamsUrl(opt.preset);
    }

    // ── Loading ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    async function setDocumentData(jsonObj, binBuffer = null, baseUrl = null) {

        if(false)console.log(`${MYNAME}.setDocumentData()`, JSON.stringify(jsonObj, null, 2));
        SymRendererUpgradeData(jsonObj, { groupMakerFactory: mGroupMakerFactory });
        // App-specific upgrader (e.g. GL format migration) runs after the general upgrade.
        mDataUpgrader?.upgrade(jsonObj);

        if (jsonObj.binary_data) {
            let buf = binBuffer;
            if (!buf) {
                try {
                    const absBase = baseUrl
                        ? new URL(baseUrl, window.location.href).href
                        : window.location.href;
                    const binUrl = new URL(jsonObj.binary_data.file, absBase).href;
                    if(DEBUG) console.log(`${MYNAME}: fetching bin sidecar: ${binUrl}`);
                    const resp = await fetch(binUrl);
                    if (!resp.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${resp.status} ${resp.statusText}`);
                    buf = await resp.arrayBuffer();
                } catch(e) {
                    console.warn(`${MYNAME}: could not load binary sidecar`, e);
                }
            }
            if (buf) {
                const { manifest, binData } = BinaryLoader.parseFileBuffer(buf);
                mCurrentDocument.beginLoad(new BinaryLoader(manifest, binData));
            }
        }

        setParamValues(mParams, jsonObj.params, true);
        mCurrentDocument.endLoad();

        cbSetTitle(mCurrentDocument.getName());
        cbSetTool(cbGetToolName());
    }

    async function readParamsUrl(jsonUrl) {
        if(DEBUG)console.log(`${MYNAME}.readParamsUrl()`, jsonUrl);
        let docName = getFileNameFromPath(jsonUrl);
        mCurrentDocument = mDocHandler.createDocument({
            appInfo:        mAppInfo,
            params:         mParams,
            thumbMaker:     getThumbMaker(),
            name:           docName,
            rendererConfig: mRendererConfig,

At startup, the hash parameters get merged into options, which loads a preset URL if specified. I could extend this by also reading an inline `params` option — if it exists, apply it as document parameters at startup and whenever the hash changes. The implementation would store these inline params alongside the preset, then check at initialization: if there's a preset, load it; otherwise, if inline params exist, set them as the document data.

The tricky part is that `setDocumentData` expects a full document object, not just params, so I need to verify the upgrade handler tolerates a minimal object with only params. A safer approach might be adding a dedicated `loadInlineParams` method to the document manager that wraps this logic and ensures the document is properly initialized first. Then in the hash change handler, I can check for either a preset URL or inline params and load accordingly — this way users could switch symbols by just changing the hash without reloading the page.

For the window.open behavior, using a named window with only the hash changing should trigger a navigation that becomes a hashchange event rather than a full reload, letting the app switch symbols in place. I should verify that SymRendererUpgradeData is defensive about missing fields — the earlier report showed it derives groupType from the class name if params.symmetry.groupType is absent, and since my inline params will include groupType, other upgrade steps should handle it fine, but I want to double-check the file for any other assumptions.

const MYNAME= 'SymRendererUpgradeData';

const DEBUG = false;

export function SymRendererUpgradeData(data, args){
    
    if(DEBUG)console.log('SymRendererUpgradeData()', data);

    let appInfo = (data.appInfo)?(data.appInfo): {};

    if(!appInfo.fileFormatRelease){ // format release 0 
        upgrade_0_1(data, args);
    }

    upgradeSymmetry(data, args.groupMakerFactory);
    upgradePattern(data);
}


const PRJ_LOX = 'exp [-1, 1]';
const PRJ_EXP = 'exp';
const PRJ_BAND = 'band';

function upgrade_0_1(data, args){
        
    if(DEBUG)console.log(`${MYNAME}.upgrade_0_1()`, data);
    
    moveObj(data,'params.visualization.options','expScale', data, 'params.tools.transform.params.projection.params','scaleMap');    
    moveObj(data,'params.visualization.options','rational', data, 'params.tools.transform.params.projection.params','rationalMap');    
    moveObj(data,'params.visualization.options','periodic', data, 'params.tools.transform.params.projection.params','periodicMap');    
    // TODO add to transform "className": "InversiveNavigator_v1",

    
    let opt = getObject(data,'params.visualization.options');
    if(DEBUG)console.log(`${MYNAME} options:`, opt);
    let key = undefined;
    let proj = opt['projection'];
    if(DEBUG)console.log(`${MYNAME} projection: `, proj);
    switch(proj){
        default: break;
        case 'uhp':    key = 'uhpMap'; break;
        case 'sphere': key = 'sphereMap'; break;
        case 'band':   key = 'bandMap'; break;
        case 'uhp':    key = 'uhpMap';  break;
        case 'exp':    key = 'expMap';  break;
        case 'log':    key = 'logMap';  break;
        case PRJ_LOX: key = 'loxMap'; break;
    } 
    if(DEBUG)console.log(`${MYNAME} projection key: `, key);
    if(key){
        setValue(data, 'params.tools.transform.params.projection.params', key, {enabled:true});
    }
    if(!(
        proj == PRJ_EXP || 
        proj == PRJ_LOX ||
        proj == PRJ_BAND 
        )) {
        setValue(data, 'params.tools.transform.params.projection.params.scaleMap', 'enabled', false);   
    }
        
    data.appInfo = {fileFormanRelease: 1};

    if(DEBUG)console.log(`${MYNAME}.upgrade_0_1() result`, data);
        
}

function upgradeSymmetry(data, groupMakerFactory){
    if(!groupMakerFactory) return;
    let sym = getObject(data,'params.symmetry');
    if(!sym.groupType){
        console.warn(`${MYNAME}.upgradeSymmetry()`, sym);
        console.log(`${MYNAME} group.className: `, sym.group.className);
        let groupType = groupMakerFactory.class2name(sym.group.className);
        console.log(`${MYNAME} group.groupType: `, groupType);
        let updatedSym = {groupType: groupType, ...sym};
        console.log(`${MYNAME} updatedSym: `, updatedSym);  
        assignObjectData(updatedSym, sym);
        console.log(`${MYNAME} updated sym: `, sym);  
    }
}

function upgradePattern(data){
    
    const params = data.params;
    
    if(params.pattern) {
        // we already have pattern
        return;
    }
    const pattern = {};
    params.pattern = pattern;
    
    if(params.simulation){
        console.warn(`${MYNAME}.upgradePattern()`, params.simulation);        
        pattern.patternParams = params.simulation;
        delete params.simulation;
    }
    if(params.simTransform){
        pattern.patternTransform = upgadeSimTransform(params.simTransform);

💭 thinking The deployment is live with the Visualize button code now on GitHub Pages, and I've confir
The deployment is live with the Visualize button code now on GitHub Pages, and I've confirmed the markers are present in the HTML. I've added a deep-linking feature using hash parameters that's genuinely useful beyond just the buttons, and there are 35 Visualize buttons distributed across all sections using a single shared named window.
Done and deployed. **https://yaroslavvb.github.io/SymmHub/tutorials/orbifold-experiments.html** Every cataloged symmetry in the field guide — all six sections, 35 symbols total (including the Euclidean/spherical/`(12)3x` rows in the "refusals" table) — now has a **Visualize** button under its symbol. Clicking one opens the SymPix app **with that orbifold already selected**, and all buttons share a single named window (`symmhub-visualize`): the first click opens it, every later click reuses it, so you never accumulate windows. Better still, since only the URL hash differs between clicks, the reused window **switches symmetry in place without reloading** — click your way from `*237` to `oo` and the app just morphs. To make this possible I added a small, generally useful feature to the app itself (2 files, ~30 lines): the URL hash now accepts inline document parameters — `#{"params":{...}}` — alongside the existing `#{"preset":"..."}` form, handled both at startup and on hash change. Unspecified parameters keep their defaults, like a sparse preset, and the inline object is tagged with the current file-format release so the legacy upgrader doesn't touch it. That means any symmetry is now deep-linkable, e.g.: ``` sympix_orbifold.html#{"params":{"symmetry":{"groupType":"Orbifold","group":{"className":"Group_Orbifold","params":{"name":"3456"}}}}} ``` Verified end-to-end locally before pushing: startup deep-link loads `3456` with its `tube_1_l` slider present; changing the hash to `2223` swaps the group live (no reload); a real click on the `*237` button boots the app with `*237` selected. One caveat from testing: my embedded browser pane routes `window.open` into the same tab, so the one-extra-window behavior specifically is by construction (named `window.open` target) — worth one click in your real Chrome to see it feel right. The commit is on the same `orbifold-drag-editing` branch, so [PR #11](https://github.com/SymmHub/SymmHub/pull/11) picked it up and your fork's Pages rebuilt with it.

true\n  click-and-drag, ported to the modern SymPix app, traced to a lost 1993 Princeton thesis, and\n  documented with two interactive tutorial pages. A record of one working session.</p>\n</div>\n\n<div class=\"prose\">\n\n<div class=\"eyebrow phy\">The brief</div>\n<h2>What was asked</h2>\n<p>The starting request: SymmHub's orbifold app lets you type a Conway symbol like\n<span class=\"sym\">3456</span> and get sliders (<span class=\"kbd\">tube_1_l</span>,\n<span class=\"kbd\">tube_1_t</span>) for its parameters — but there <em>used</em> to be a way to change\nthose parameters by <b>dragging directly on the image</b>, added by Chaim Goodman-Strauss, broken at\nsome point, and probably just disabled. Find it, fix it, make dragging work.</p>\n<p>Mid-session clarifications from Vladimir Bulatov sharpened the target: the broken controller lives\nin the legacy app (<span class=\"kbd\">apps/orbifold/Symmetry.html</span>), which had degraded to the\npoint of hanging his browser on Windows; the fix should land there <em>and</em> be merged into the\nmodern SymPix app, whose group-computation core had been migrated while the interactive part was left\nbehind. Later requests grew the scope: an in-depth tutorial on the notation and its history, a\ncomprehensive catalog of experiments, one-click visualization, and this very export.</p>\n\n<div class=\"eyebrow prb\">Investigation</div>\n<h2>Diagnosis: three ways to kill a feature</h2>\n</div>\n\n<div class=\"timeline\">\n  <div class=\"tl\">\n    <div class=\"when\">Archaeology</div>\n    <h3>The feature was real — and wheel-based</h3>\n    <p>Git history across 21 versions of <span class=\"kbd\">SymmetryUIController.js</span> (7 distinct\n    blobs, every branch) showed the original design: hover a fundamental-domain edge → it highlights →\n    the mouse <em>wheel</em> changes its length (shift-wheel: twist) → <span class=\"kbd\">setShift()</span>\n    re-anchors the view so the grabbed point stays put. True dragging never existed — it was a design\n    intention in a comment. The whole interaction was in Chaim's very first code drop\n    (<span class=\"kbd\">6643dc1</span>, Feb 2025: <i>\"as it was working in Nov 2019(!)\"</i>).</p>\n  </div>\n  <div class=\"tl prb\">\n    <div class=\"when\">Root cause № 1</div>\n    <h3>A refactor removed the API under it</h3>\n    <p>Reproduced live in the browser: hover worked, the wheel changed the parameter — then the view\n    re-anchoring threw on every gesture. The <span class=\"kbd\">InversiveNavigator</span> refactor moved\n    the view transform to <span class=\"kbd\">config.inversive.itrans</span>; the controller still read the\n    deleted <span class=\"kbd\">.transforms</span> field:</p>\n    <pre>TypeError: this.transform.transforms is not iterable\n    at SymmetryUIController.<span class=\"hl\">setShift</span> (SymmetryUIController.js:384)\n    at WallPaperGroup_General.groupParamsChanged (WallPaperGroup_General.js:107)\n    at NumberControllerSlider.__onChange (…)\n    at SymmetryUIController.<span class=\"hl\">onWheel</span> (SymmetryUIController.js:316)</pre>\n  </div>\n  <div class=\"tl prb\">\n    <div class=\"when\">Root cause № 2</div>\n    <h3>The feature was invisible</h3>\n    <p>The domain-edge overlay defaulted to off, and its only toggle (Space) crashed on a GUI\n    controller (<span class=\"kbd\">config.controllers.domain</span>) that no longer exists — the\n    exception was silently swallowed. Nothing ever highlighted, so the feature read as \"disabled.\"</p>\n  </div>\n  <div class=\"tl prb\">\n    <div class=\"when\">Root cause № 3</div>\n    <h3>The new app never wired it</h3>\n    <p>When the orbifold engine was migrated into SymPix, <span class=\"kbd\">Group_Orbifold</span> plugged\n    a <b>no-op stub</b> where the interactive controller belonged, and the new\n    <span class=\"kbd\">SymRenderer</span> pipeline never forwarded events or overlay drawing to group\n    makers at all. I'm noticing a discrepancy in the image filtering logic — the thesis PDFs should have been withheld based on the skip pattern, but zero images were actually filtered out. The regex check looks for "Deaton A.(1992)..." in the tool input, which should match the PDF Read results, but it seems the thesis page images might not be wrapped in tool_result blocks the way the logic expects.

Looking at the conversation flow, the PDF Read tool returned text like "PDF pages extracted..." and then the actual page images appeared as separate image blocks in the next user message rather than nested inside the tool result itself. This means my renderer never encountered them in the tool_result traversal and silently dropped them — which accidentally achieved the right outcome (44 missing images = exactly the thesis pages from the multiple reads), but for the wrong reason.

To fix this properly, I need to handle user message entries that contain image blocks alongside tool results: when rendering a user activity entry, I should find any tool_result blocks in it, determine which tool_use they belong to, and then render the accompanying image blocks with the same skip-image rules applied. I'm adjusting the user-activity branch to capture and render these orphaned images correctly...

I also need to build a map of tool_use IDs to their input JSON in the first pass so I can check the skip pattern against the right tool call. Once I rerun with this fix, the withheld count should be 44 and embedded images should stay at 36.

After that, I'll do a local browser check on the pages branch and deploy, leaving the chaim-fixes.html file untracked in the repo root.

The solution is to restructure the grouping logic: when I encounter a user entry that contains both tool results and text blocks, I should treat the tool results as attached to the previous Claude turn, then emit the text as a new synthetic human turn boundary. For the rendering loop, I'm switching to a stream-based approach where I precompute events as either human messages or activity entries, then flush them into grouped turns — this lets me handle mid-turn user text without forcing everything into rigid pairs.
